DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
This study recommends a district-wide weekly food waste collection from April 2027. It rests on three claims: a six-month pilot showed participation held up in houses and flats alike; treatment can happen locally at Brookfield; and the net cost of about £490,000 is fully covered by new-burdens funding.

Several things are sound:
- **The pilot design.** Six months, 4,000 households and a housing mix that matches the district (20% flats in both) is a strong base for projections.
- **The arithmetic.** Table 2 adds up, the vehicle depreciation is correct, and the £74/tonne disposal saving is calculated correctly.
- **Contamination.** Checking contamination at the treatment plant is good practice.
- **The timeline.** Working back from the vehicle lead time is the right approach.

However, the pilot data contradict two of the study's central claims. The projection also uses a participation rate the pilot never achieved, and the treatment plant can't take the projected tonnage. With those corrected, the service is probably not fully funded.

## 1. Participation did not hold up in flats

Table 1 shows **66% in houses and 21% in flats**. Houses participated at three times the rate of flats. The text calls this "broadly similar" and uses it to justify a uniform service. That claim appears in the pilot section, the recommendation and the author's note, and the table contradicts it each time.

The pilot evidence actually points to the opposite conclusion: flats need a different approach. Common options include communal food bins in bin stores, different containers, and targeted communications. With about 10,400 flats in the district, this needs its own plan and its own cost line.

## 2. The projection uses 64% participation, but the pilot achieved 57%

The study says it applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate". The pilot's overall rate was 57% (2,280 of 4,000). The 1.9 kg figure is also the houses-only yield; the combined figure is about 1.86 kg.

The pilot's mix matches the district's, so the pilot rates can be applied by housing type:

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ~2,710 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ~160 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **~2,870** |

That is about **2,870 tonnes, not 3,290**, an overstatement of about 13%. The pilot also ran January to June, while the service was new. Participation often drops off after launch, so even 2,870 may be optimistic without ongoing communications.

## 3. Brookfield can take only 1,800 tonnes

The study notes that Brookfield's contracted capacity is 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029. It then calculates the whole saving as if every projected tonne goes there at £38. Even the corrected 2,870 tonnes leaves about **1,070 tonnes a year without local treatment** for at least two years.

The study has to say where that tonnage goes:
- **To the next plant, 46 miles away.** The gate fee is unknown. Collection vehicles can't make a 92-mile round trip without losing collection time, so this probably means a transfer station and onward haulage, at extra cost.
- **To incineration.** If the food waste stays in the residual stream, it earns no saving.

"Treatment is local" is therefore true for less than two-thirds of the corrected tonnage.

## 4. The funding position after correction

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | vs £520k allocation |
|---|---|---|---|
| As stated (3,290 t, all to Brookfield) | £243,000 | £490,400 | +£30k headroom |
| Corrected tonnage, all to Brookfield (ignores the capacity cap) | ~£212,000 | ~£521,000 | Already slightly over |
| Corrected tonnage, 1,800 t to Brookfield, excess incinerated | ~£133,000 | ~£600,000 | **~£80k short** |

The third row is the realistic position until 2029 unless an alternative is costed. Alternative treatment for the excess would sit somewhere between the second and third rows, after haulage costs. These figures use the study's own cost base, which section 5 suggests is also incomplete.

The £520,000 is also a *provisional* allocation that the Government has "indicated". The study should not describe the service as "fully funded" until the allocation is confirmed. It also needs a plan for any shortfall.

## 5. Cost lines that are missing or unclear

The study calls the costs "complete", but several items are absent or ambiguous:
- **Crew costs.** Is £34,000 per operative a salary or the full cost to the Council? If it excludes employer's National Insurance and pension, crew costs could be roughly £100,000 higher.
- **Cover.** Twelve operatives with no allowance for holidays or sickness won't sustain a weekly service. Agency or relief staff typically add 10–15%.
- **Spare vehicle.** Six vehicles and no spare means every breakdown causes missed collections.
- **Supervision and overheads.** Round management, depot space, insurance and the dedicated phone line and web page are not costed.
- **Capital and one-off costs.** About £990,000 for vehicles plus caddies for 52,000 households must be paid up front. The financing cost, the source of the capital, and recruitment and training costs are not shown.
- **Round capacity.** Six crews covering 52,000 households a week is about 1,700 households per crew per day. Check this against the pilot's actual productivity before ordering vehicles, since too few vehicles is costly to fix after delivery.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Satisfaction.** The 81% figure needs the survey's response rate. Non-participants, including most flats, are probably under-represented.
- **Statutory deadline.** For most English councils, the start date for weekly food waste collection was 31 March 2026. If Thornbury has a transitional arrangement allowing a 2027 start, the study should say so. If not, the Council is already late, which strengthens the case for acting quickly but should be stated.
- **Caddy procurement.** Delivering caddies to 52,000 households in March 2027 needs an ordering deadline in the timetable, alongside the vehicle order.

## On the author's description

| Claim | What the document shows |
|---|---|
| "Participation held up across houses and flats" | 66% vs 21% |
| Projection based on pilot behaviour | It uses 64%; the pilot's overall rate was 57% |
| "Treatment is local" | Only for 1,800 of the ~2,870 tonnes, until 2029 |
| "Every cost line is shown" | On-costs, cover, a spare vehicle, overheads and capital financing are missing or unclear |
| "Fully covered" by the allocation | The allocation is provisional, and with corrected figures the net cost probably exceeds it |

## Recommendation

The service is a legal requirement, so Cabinet's decision is about design and budget, not whether to proceed. Two of the study's conclusions, uniform service design and full funding, depend on readings the data don't support.

A reasonable route is for Cabinet to **authorise the vehicle order now** to protect the April 2027 start, after the round capacity is checked. It should then ask for a revised business case before the budget is set, covering:
1. A tonnage projection by housing type, of about 2,870 t, with a sensitivity for post-launch drop-off.
2. A separate collection approach and cost line for flats.
3. A costed treatment plan for the tonnage above Brookfield's 1,800 t limit until 2029.
4. Full costs: on-costs, cover, a spare vehicle, supervision, overheads, capital financing and one-off costs.
5. The funding position on corrected figures, with a contingency if the confirmed allocation is lower.
